source.title: Gamma-ray emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. New discoveries and open questions

accepted.question_text: Gamma-ray-emitting radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies are Seyfert active galactic nuclei characterized by narrow permitted Hβ lines, [OIII]/Hβ < 3, an Fe II bump, strong X-ray variability, steep X-ray spectra, substantial soft X-ray excess, relatively small central black-hole masses, high accretion rates, and an expected association with spiral hosts. Do the five radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies detected by Fermi-LAT in gamma rays constitute a distinct third class of active galactic nuclei with relativistic jets, in addition to blazars and radio galaxies, and what is the physical nature of that class?
accepted.context_brief: AGN class status of gamma-ray radio-loud NLSy1s

evidence.quote: The discovery of γ-ray emission from 5 radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies revealed the presence of a possible emerging third class of AGNs with relativistic jets, in addition to blazars and radio galaxies.

NLSy1 is a class of AGN identified by Osterbrock & Pogge (1985) and characterized by their optical properties: narrow permitted lines (FWHM (Hβ) < 2000 km s−1) emitted from the broad line region (BLR), [OIII]/Hβ < 3, and a bump due to Fe II.

They also exhibit strong X-ray variability, steep X-ray spectra, and substantial soft X-ray excess. These characteristics point to systems with smaller masses of the central black hole (BH = 10^6–10^8 M⊙) and higher accretion rates (close to or above the Eddington limit) with respect to blazars and radio galaxies.

Considering also that NLSy1s are thought to be hosted in spiral galaxies, their detection in γ rays poses intriguing questions about the nature of these sources, the production of relativistic jets, the mechanisms of high-energy emission, and the cosmological evolution of radio-loud AGN.

accepted.question_text: For the five radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies detected by Fermi-LAT, whose apparent isotropic luminosities in the 0.1–100 GeV band are about 10^44–10^47 erg s−1 and therefore blazar-like, are the high gamma-ray luminosities mainly produced because the relativistic jet is viewed at a small angle and has a high beaming factor?

evidence.quote: So far five radio-loud NLSy1 galaxies have been detected at high significance by Fermi-LAT: 1H 0323+342, SBS 0846+513, PMN J0948+0022, PKS 1502+036, and PKS 2004−447.

Their average apparent isotropic luminosity in the 0.1–100 GeV energy band is between 10^44 erg s−1 and 10^47 erg s−1, a range of values typical of blazars. This could be an indication of a small viewing angle with respect to the jet axis and thus a high beaming factor for the γ-ray emission, similarly to blazars.

accepted.question_text: In the radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy PKS 1502+036, how can evidence for relativistic boosting—a one-sided radio structure and radio spectral variability—be reconciled with the absence of detected apparent superluminal motion at 15 GHz in VLBA observations from 2002 to 2012?

evidence.quote: When observed in the radio band with the high angular resolution provided by the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA), the γ-ray emitting NLSy1s usually show a pc-scale core-jet structure. This is the case of SBS 0846+513, PKS 1502+036, and PMN J0948+0022, although in the last two sources the jet structure is faint.

On the contrary, VLBA observations did not detect apparent superluminal motion at 15 GHz for PKS 1502+036 during 2002–2012, although the radio spectral variability and the one-sided structure seem to require the presence of boosting effects in a relativistic jet.

accepted.question_text: What physical and temporal connection links radio-band emission and gamma-ray emission in the radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies SBS 0846+513 and PMN J0948+0022, given that their gamma-ray flares and radio flares do not show similar behavior?

evidence.quote: A complex connection between the radio and γ-ray emission was observed for SBS 0846+513 and PMN J0948+0022, where γ-ray and radio flares have not a similar behaviour.

accepted.question_text: What physical parameters determine whether a radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy can form an efficient relativistic jet: is a large central black-hole mass required, or can the relatively small black-hole masses traditionally estimated for gamma-ray-emitting radio-loud NLSy1s, about 10^7–10^8 solar masses, still produce powerful jets?

evidence.quote: The physical parameters that drive the jet formation are still under debate. An important parameter could be the BH mass, with only large masses allowing an efficient jet formation.

Therefore one of the most surprising fact related to the discovery of γ-ray emission from radio-loud NLSy1s was the production of a relativistic jet in objects with a relatively small BH mass (10^7–10^8 M⊙; Yuan et al. 2008).
This is another indication that radio-loud NLSy1s are able to host relativistic jets as powerful as those in blazars.

accepted.question_text: If corrected estimates place black-hole masses in radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies as high as 10^8–10^9 solar masses, including about 10^9 solar masses for PMN J0948+0022 and 2×10^8 solar masses for PKS 1502+036, how can such large black holes exist in galaxies that are thought to be spiral hosts?
accepted.context_brief: Massive black holes in spiral hosts

evidence.quote: Recently, Calderone et al. (2013) modelling the optical/UV data of some radio-loud NLSy1s with a Shakura & Sunyaev disc spectrum estimated BH masses higher than 10^8 M⊙. In particular, they derived a BH mass of 10^9 M⊙ and 2×10^8 M⊙ for PMN J0948+0022 and PKS 1502+036, respectively, in agreement with the typical BH mass of blazars.

This may solve the problem of the minimum BH mass predicted in different scenarios of relativistic jet formation and development, but introduces a new issue. If the BH mass of these NLSy1s is 10^8-10^9 M⊙, how is it possible to have such a large BH mass in a spiral galaxy?

Considering also that NLSy1s are thought to be hosted in spiral galaxies, their detection in γ rays poses intriguing questions about the nature of these sources, the production of relativistic jets, the mechanisms of high-energy emission, and the cosmological evolution of radio-loud AGN.

accepted.question_text: What are the host-galaxy morphologies of gamma-ray-emitting radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies, and can their relativistic jets be explained by strong merger activity rather than ordinary spiral-galaxy evolution, given that only 1H 0323+342 has a clearly detected host and observations of it have been interpreted either as spiral arms or as merger residual structure?

evidence.quote: Unfortunately only very sparse observations of the host galaxy of radio-loud NLSy1s are available up to now. Among the NLSy1s detected by LAT only for the closest one, 1H 0323+342, the host galaxy was clearly detected.

Hubble Space Telescope and Nordic Optical Telescope observations seem to reveal a one-armed galaxy morphology or a circumnuclear ring, respectively, suggesting two possibilities: the spiral arms of the host galaxy or the residual of a galaxy merging. Thus the possibility that the production of relativistic jets in these objects could be due to strong merger activity, unusual in disc/spiral galaxies, cannot be ruled out.

accepted.question_text: Can the modified spin paradigm for relativistic jet production accommodate radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies if these systems are hosted by spiral galaxies: specifically, how can a central supermassive black hole in such a system acquire enough spin for efficient jet production when the paradigm associates high average spin and efficient spin-up with elliptical galaxies and major mergers?
accepted.context_brief: Modified spin paradigm in spiral-host NLSy1s

evidence.quote: According to the “modified spin paradigm”, another fundamental parameter for the efficiency of a relativistic jet production should be the BH spin, with SMBHs in elliptical galaxies having on average much larger spins than SMBHs in spiral galaxies.

This is due to the fact that the spiral galaxies are characterized by multiple accretion events with random angular momentum orientation and small increments of mass, while elliptical galaxies undergo at least one major merger with large matter accretion triggering an efficient spin-up of the SMBH.
The accretion rate (thus the mass) and the spin of the BH seem to be related to the host galaxy, leading to the hypothesis that relativistic jets can form only in elliptical galaxy.

Considering also that NLSy1s are thought to be hosted in spiral galaxies, their detection in γ rays poses intriguing questions about the nature of these sources, the production of relativistic jets, the mechanisms of high-energy emission, and the cosmological evolution of radio-loud AGN.

accepted.question_text: Why is the fraction of radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies so small compared with radio-loud quasars, and is the rarity explained by only some NLSy1 galaxies experiencing high-accretion episodes that last long enough to spin up their central black holes?
accepted.context_brief: Rarity and evolutionary duration of radio-loud NLSy1s

evidence.quote: NLSy1s are generally radio-quiet (radio-loudness R < 10), with only a small fraction of them (<7%; Komossa et al. 2006) classified as radio-loud, and objects with high values of radio-loudness (R > 100) are even more sparse (∼2.5%), while generally ∼15% of quasars are radio-loud.

The larger BH masses of radio-loud NLSy1s with respect to radio-quiet NLSy1s could be related to prolonged accretion episodes that can spin-up the BHs. In this context, the small fraction of radio-loud NLSy1s with respect to radio-loud quasars could be an indication that not in all of the former the high-accretion regime lasted long enough to spin-up the central BH.
